title: Mex the Dog: The Story of OU's Beloved Early Sooner Mascot
question: Who was Mex the Dog, the Oklahoma Sooners mascot?
answer: Mex was a dog found as a pup near the Mexican border in 1914 by Army medic Mott Keys, who later brought him to OU. Mex served as a Sooner mascot into the 1920s, died April 30, 1928, and was buried near Owen Field.
summary: Mex the Dog, found near the Mexican border in 1914, became OU's beloved mascot. He died in April 1928, and OU closed for his funeral near Owen Field.
body: Long before the Sooner Schooner, Oklahoma's sidelines belonged to a scrappy little dog named Mex. In 1914, during the unrest of the Mexican Revolution, Army field hospital medic Mott Keys was stationed near Laredo, Texas, when he found a litter of abandoned pups on the Mexican side of the border. One of them was adopted as his company's mascot. When Keys later enrolled at OU, Mex came with him.

Mex made himself at home at the Kappa Sigma house and quickly became the most famous dog in the state. At games he wore a red sweater marked with a big O, and he had a real job: chasing stray dogs off the field in an era when it was easy for animals and people to wander in. He also entertained crowds by catching hedge apples between quarters.

His most famous adventure came on a road trip in the 1920s, when Mex failed to reboard the team train during a stop in Arkansas City, Kansas. OU's account places it in October 1924, on the way to a 28-0 loss at Drake, and a local paper blamed the defeat on the missing mascot. Mex was later found pacing the station platform, and OU alumni brought him back to the team.

Mex died of old age on April 30, 1928. The campus newspaper reported he had been a mascot for 13 years, and the university closed for his funeral on May 2, with the RUF/NEKS, the Jazz Hounds and the band joining the procession. He was buried at the north edge of Owen Field, which means part of OU's football history literally rests on the stadium grounds.
